**Mount Gretna, Pennsylvania – A Concise Yet Detailed History**

---

### 1. Location & Basic Facts
- **Borough:** Mount Gretna  
- **County:** Lebanon County, Pennsylvania  
- **Coordinates:** 40°14′47″N 76°28′22″W (≈40.24639° N, ‑76.47278° W)  
- **ZIP code:** 17064 | Area code: 717  
- **Population (2020):** 193 residents (the borough’s “surrounding area” is estimated at ~1,500–2,500 during summer)  

The town sits in the Conewago Hills, just west of Philadelphia, in a wooded, chestnut‑tree forested valley.

---

### 2. Unique Founding

| Year | Event | Details |
|------|-------|---------|
| **1883** | Discovery | A small woodland park was found along the *extinct* Cornwall and Lebanon Railroad, which linked the Reading Railroad to the Pennsylvania Railroad near Elizabethtown. President Benjamin Harrison stopped there to detrain trains and picnicked. |
| **1883 (Sept 21)** | First public mention | The name **“Mount Gretna”** appears in the *Lebanon Daily News*; it was suggested by the wife of **Hugh Maxwell**, an official of the Cornwall and Lebanon Railroad. |
| **1885** | National Guard encampment begins | The Pennsylvania National Guard started its first permanent training site at Mount Gretna. |
| **1889** | Land acquisition & narrow‑gauge railroad | Iron‑foundry heir **Robert H. Coleman** (great‑grandson of an Irish Revolutionary munitions supplier) bought most of the land and built a narrow‑gauge railroad to carry visitors up Governor Dick Hill. |
| **1892** | Chautauqua establishment | A group of **Evangelical United Brethren** members chose the area for a “Chautauqua.” They laid out lots, erected a vaulted conical‑roofed outdoor auditorium, a Greek temple for the Literary and Scientific Circle, and hired builder **John Cilley**. The first cottages, Hall of Philosophy, and Tabernacle were constructed. |
| **1907** | Major land purchase | Coleman further expanded his holdings, including parcels given to the Chautauqua group. |

> *Sources:* Wikipedia entry notes the borough was “founded by the Pennsylvania Chautauqua Society…by the 1890s” and lists “settled 1889, incorporated 1926”【webpage_scraping】; the official site describes the 1883 discovery, the name origin, and the 1885 National Guard encampment【mtgretna.com/about-gretna/our-history/】; CBS News recounts Coleman’s role and the 1892 Chautauqua launch【www.cbsnews.com/pittsburgh/news/pennsylvania-chautauqua-mount-gretna/】.

---

### 3. Subdivisions / Neighborhoods

Mount Gretna is divided into **seven distinct sections** (some borders extend into South Londonderry Township):

1. **Mount Gretna Heights** – home to the **Mount Gretna Inn**.  
2. **Stoberdale** – residential area.  
3. **Campmeeting** – contains the **Tabernacle** (church) and campground.  
4. **Chautauqua** – post office, **Playhouse**, playground, and **Jigger Shop** ice‑cream parlor.  
5. **Timber Hills** – includes the **Timbers Restaurant** and surrounding hillside.  
6. **Conewago Hill / Timber Bridge / Conewago Lake** – not technically within the borough but part of the local recreation zone.  
7. **Culture Gulch** – colloquial nickname for the tightly packed, privately owned cottages.

These neighborhoods each retain their own identity, with many cottages still maintained in early‑20th‑century styles.

---

### 4. Cultural History

- **Chautauqua Movement** – Modeled on the original Chautauqua Institution (New York, 1874). Initiated in 1892; attracted teachers, Sunday‑school groups, and “book clubs,” reading circles, scientific lectures, and literary societies.  
- **Amusement Park Era** – Early attractions included a **carousel**, a primitive **roller coaster called a “switch‑back,”** a dancing pavilion, and a stone fountain.  
- **Arts & Education** – Hall of Philosophy (completed 1909) hosted lectures, classes, and the “Hall of Philosophy” gatherings; the **Gretna Theatre** (opened 1927) became one of the few professional summer‑stock theatres in the U.S.; the **Playhouse** continued performances.  
- **Music & Performance** – Jazz, chamber music, bluegrass duos, and “International Make Music on Your Porch Day” are regular summer events.  
- **Art Shows** – The **First Annual Outdoor Art Show** (1976) launched a thriving artist scene featuring Bruce Johnson, Reed Dixon, John Wenzler, and later Carl Ellenberger.  
- **Decline & Revival** – Automobile travel, the Great Depression, and WWII reduced popularity; the amusement park closed in the 1920s, hotels emptied, and the narrow‑gauge railroad was abandoned. A modern revival began in the 1970s with the art show and chamber‑music series, now listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

> *Sources:* AP News describes the “54‑page pamphlet” of summer programs, the “culture gulch” nickname, and the resurgence in the 1970s【apnews.com/article/mount-gretna-pennsylvania-chautauqua-80cf63fed0d2641fff09f5671a6c4b0】; CBS News gives details on inaugural classes, attendance (~8,800), and the Chautauqua craze peaking in 1907【www.cbsnews.com/pittsburgh/news/pennsylvania-chautauqua-mount-gretna/】.

---

### 5. Religious History

- **Evangelical United Brethren** organized the first Chautauqua in 1892 and built the **Tabernacle** for worship and Bible meetings.  
- A **Greek temple** was erected for the Chautauqua Literary and Scientific Circle.  
- The **old jail** on the second floor of the Hall of Philosophy served as a community hub when mail delivery was suspended.  
- After the town’s decline, the **Pennsylvania Chautauqua Foundation** purchased the 18.4‑acre **Soldier’s Field** in 2019 to preserve it as a living memorial to the National Guard era.  
- The foundation’s $470,000 revitalization project (dedicated June 2025) adds a paved walking trail, a foot bridge over Conewago Creek (the “28th Iron Division Bridge”), and interpretive signage.

> *Source:* Official site notes the Tabernacle construction and the 1890s ice‑cream shop; CBS News mentions Bible studies and the Tabernacle’s role【mtgretna.com/about-gretna/our-history/】【www.cbsnews.com/pittsburgh/news/pennsylvania-chautauqua-mount-gretna/】.

---

### 6. Military History

- **Training Site Since 1885** – The Pennsylvania National Guard held its first permanent encampment at Mount Gretna.  
- **Spanish‑American War Mobilization (April 25, 1898)** – Governor Daniel Hastings ordered the National Guard to report; nearly 9,000 troops arrived, 97 % volunteered; 12,000 officers and men were mustered into federal service between May 6 and July 22, 1898. The camp was initially called **“Camp Hastings.”**  
- **Expansion (late 1920s)** – The site grew to ~2,800 acres; artillery and motorized vehicles required more space.  
- **Transfer to Fort Indiantown Gap** – In 1931 authorization was granted to acquire land in northern Lebanon County; training resumed in 1932. By 1940 the **17,000‑acre Indiantown Gap Military Reservation** was completed and leased to the U.S. Army, officially dedicated **March 3, 1941**.  
- **Last Years (pre‑WWII)** – About 300 buildings were disassembled and reassembled; a Victorian‑style range house (built 1890) was moved to Indiantown Gap in 1938.  
- **Soldier’s Field Project (2020s)** – The Pennsylvania Chautauqua Foundation restored the former training ground into a community green space, adding a walking path, a foot bridge over Conewago Creek, and interpretive markers. Volunteers continue projects such as native‑plant planting and meadow restoration.

> *Source:* FTIG article details the 1885 start, 1898 war mobilization, growth to 2,800 acres, transfer to Fort Indiantown Gap, 1940 completion, and the 2025 Soldier’s Field revitalization【www.ftig.ng.mil/About-Us/News/Article/4232222/mount-gretna-fort-indiantown-gaps-predecessor/】.

---

### 7. Summer Recreation Site Status

Mount Gretna is a **year‑round summer retreat** whose population roughly doubles in June–August. Key features:

- **Lake Conewago** – Victorian‑era bathhouse with high‑dive floating docks, sandy beach, swimming, canoeing.  
- **Porches & Front Street** – Iconic front porches define the town; strict rules limit lawn mowers and tree trimming.  
- **Recreation Facilities** – Roller rink (open‑air playhouse), miniature golf course, boating, kayak/paddleboard rentals.  
- **Entertainment** – Juried art shows (third weekend of August), jazz/chamber‑music concerts, lecture series, book reviews, “International Make Music on Your Porch Day.”  
- **Events Calendar** – Cooking lessons, nature walks, yoga, professorial talks, flamenco dance lessons, Rachel Carson reenactments, etc.  
- **Community Hub** – Post office serves double duty; many cottages lack mail delivery.

> *Source:* CBS News describes the “summer camp” atmosphere, the porch culture, and the double‑use of the post office【www.cbsnews.com/pittsburgh/news/pennsylvania-chautauqua-mount-gretna/】.

---

| **2000s–Present** | **Soldier’s Field** restoration, **Timbers Restaurant & Dinner Theatre**, **Jigger Shop** ice‑cream parlor (operating since 1890s), **Gretna Theatre** (one of America’s oldest professional summer stock theatres). |

> *Sources:* Wikipedia geography section; official site’s “Our History” detailing early amusements and hotels; AP News describing the 54‑page program and 1909 Hall of Philosophy; Timbers Restaurant listing; Jigger Shop website noting operation since 1895; Gretna Theatre description as one of the oldest summer stock theatres【webpage_scraping】【jiggershop.com】【gretnatheatre.org】.

---

### 10. Recent Developments (2020s)

- **Volunteer Projects**: Native‑plant planting, meadow creation, bird‑club habitat (Purple Martin house).  
- **Ongoing Community Programs**: Art shows, chamber‑music/jazz concerts, “Make Music on Your Porch Day,” cooking lessons, nature walks, yoga.

> *Source:* FTIG article on the Soldier’s Field project and the Foundation’s purchase【www.ftig.ng.mil/About-Us/News/Article/4232222/mount-gretna-fort-indiantown-gaps-predecessor/】.

---

## Summary

Mount Gretna began as a quiet woodland picnic stop in 1883, quickly becoming a **rail‑linked summer resort** thanks to President Harrison’s visits. Its **unique blend of Chautauqua education, national‑guard training, and rustic mountain charm** gave rise to a vibrant summer culture—characterized by porches, art shows, live music, and a tight‑knit community of privately owned cottages. The town’s **military legacy** is anchored by the Pennsylvania National Guard’s long‑standing encampments, the Spanish‑American War mobilization, and the eventual conversion of the site into **Fort Indiantown Gap** and the modern **Soldier’s Field** restoration. Today, Mount Gretna thrives as a **summer recreation haven** with Lake Conewago, historic hotels, the Hall of Philosophy, and a lively arts scene, while retaining several historic businesses dating back to the late 19th century.

**Mount Gretna, Pennsylvania – A Concise Yet Detailed History**

---

### 1. Location & Basic Facts
- **Borough:** Mount Gretna  
- **County:** Lebanon County, Pennsylvania  
- **Coordinates:** 40°14′47″N 76°28′22″W (≈40.24639° N, ‑76.47278° W)  
- **ZIP code:** 17064 | Area code: 717  
- **Population (2020):** 193 residents (the borough’s “surrounding area” is estimated at ~1,500–2,500 during summer)  

The town sits in the Conewago Hills, just west of Philadelphia, in a wooded, chestnut‑tree forested valley.

---

### 2. Unique Founding

| Year | Event | Details |
|------|-------|---------|
| **1883** | Discovery | A small woodland park was found along the *extinct* Cornwall and Lebanon Railroad, which linked the Reading Railroad to the Pennsylvania Railroad near Elizabethtown. President Benjamin Harrison stopped there to detrain trains and picnicked. |
| **1883 (Sept 21)** | First public mention | The name **“Mount Gretna”** appears in the *Lebanon Daily News*; it was suggested by the wife of **Hugh Maxwell**, an official of the Cornwall and Lebanon Railroad. |
| **1885** | National Guard encampment begins | The Pennsylvania National Guard started its first permanent training site at Mount Gretna. |
| **1889** | Land acquisition & narrow‑gauge railroad | Iron‑foundry heir **Robert H. Coleman** (great‑grandson of an Irish Revolutionary munitions supplier) bought most of the land and built a narrow‑gauge railroad to carry visitors up Governor Dick Hill. |
| **1892** | Chautauqua establishment | A group of **Evangelical United Brethren** members chose the area for a “Chautauqua.” They laid out lots, erected a vaulted conical‑roofed outdoor auditorium, a Greek temple for the Literary and Scientific Circle, and hired builder **John Cilley**. The first cottages, Hall of Philosophy, and Tabernacle were constructed. |
| **1907** | Major land purchase | Coleman further expanded his holdings, including parcels given to the Chautauqua group. |

> *Sources:* Wikipedia entry notes the borough was “founded by the Pennsylvania Chautauqua Society…by the 1890s” and lists “settled 1889, incorporated 1926”【webpage_scraping】; the official site describes the 1883 discovery, the name origin, and the 1885 National Guard encampment【mtgretna.com/about-gretna/our-history/】; CBS News recounts Coleman’s role and the 1892 Chautauqua launch【www.cbsnews.com/pittsburgh/news/pennsylvania-chautauqua-mount-gretna/】.

---

### 3. Subdivisions / Neighborhoods

Mount Gretna is divided into **seven distinct sections** (some borders extend into South Londonderry Township):

1. **Mount Gretna Heights** – home to the **Mount Gretna Inn**.  
2. **Stoberdale** – residential area.  
3. **Campmeeting** – contains the **Tabernacle** (church) and campground.  
4. **Chautauqua** – post office, **Playhouse**, playground, and **Jigger Shop** ice‑cream parlor.  
5. **Timber Hills** – includes the **Timbers Restaurant** and surrounding hillside.  
6. **Conewago Hill / Timber Bridge / Conewago Lake** – not technically within the borough but part of the local recreation zone.  
7. **Culture Gulch** – colloquial nickname for the tightly packed, privately owned cottages.

These neighborhoods each retain their own identity, with many cottages still maintained in early‑20th‑century styles.

---

### 4. Cultural History

- **Chautauqua Movement** – Modeled on the original Chautauqua Institution (New York, 1874). Initiated in 1892; attracted teachers, Sunday‑school groups, and “book clubs,” reading circles, scientific lectures, and literary societies.  
- **Amusement Park Era** – Early attractions included a **carousel**, a primitive **roller coaster called a “switch‑back,”** a dancing pavilion, and a stone fountain.  
- **Arts & Education** – Hall of Philosophy (completed 1909) hosted lectures, classes, and the “Hall of Philosophy” gatherings; the **Gretna Theatre** (opened 1927) became one of the few professional summer‑stock theatres in the U.S.; the **Playhouse** continued performances.  
- **Music & Performance** – Jazz, chamber music, bluegrass duos, and “International Make Music on Your Porch Day” are regular summer events.  
- **Art Shows** – The **First Annual Outdoor Art Show** (1976) launched a thriving artist scene featuring Bruce Johnson, Reed Dixon, John Wenzler, and later Carl Ellenberger.  
- **Decline & Revival** – Automobile travel, the Great Depression, and WWII reduced popularity; the amusement park closed in the 1920s, hotels emptied, and the narrow‑gauge railroad was abandoned. A modern revival began in the 1970s with the art show and chamber‑music series, now listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

> *Sources:* AP News describes the “54‑page pamphlet” of summer programs, the “culture gulch” nickname, and the resurgence in the 1970s【apnews.com/article/mount-gretna-pennsylvania-chautauqua-80cf63fed0d2641fff09f5671a6c4b0】; CBS News gives details on inaugural classes, attendance (~8,800), and the Chautauqua craze peaking in 1907【www.cbsnews.com/pittsburgh/news/pennsylvania-chautauqua-mount-gretna/】.

---

### 5. Religious History

- **Evangelical United Brethren** organized the first Chautauqua in 1892 and built the **Tabernacle** for worship and Bible meetings.  
- A **Greek temple** was erected for the Chautauqua Literary and Scientific Circle.  
- The **old jail** on the second floor of the Hall of Philosophy served as a community hub when mail delivery was suspended.  
- After the town’s decline, the **Pennsylvania Chautauqua Foundation** purchased the 18.4‑acre **Soldier’s Field** in 2019 to preserve it as a living memorial to the National Guard era.  
- The foundation’s $470,000 revitalization project (dedicated June 2025) adds a paved walking trail, a foot bridge over Conewago Creek (the “28th Iron Division Bridge”), and interpretive signage.

> *Source:* Official site notes the Tabernacle construction and the 1890s ice‑cream shop; CBS News mentions Bible studies and the Tabernacle’s role【mtgretna.com/about-gretna/our-history/】【www.cbsnews.com/pittsburgh/news/pennsylvania-chautauqua-mount-gretna/】.

---

### 6. Military History

- **Training Site Since 1885** – The Pennsylvania National Guard held its first permanent encampment at Mount Gretna.  
- **Spanish‑American War Mobilization (April 25, 1898)** – Governor Daniel Hastings ordered the National Guard to report; nearly 9,000 troops arrived, 97 % volunteered; 12,000 officers and men were mustered into federal service between May 6 and July 22, 1898. The camp was initially called **“Camp Hastings.”**  
- **Expansion (late 1920s)** – The site grew to ~2,800 acres; artillery and motorized vehicles required more space.  
- **Transfer to Fort Indiantown Gap** – In 1931 authorization was granted to acquire land in northern Lebanon County; training resumed in 1932. By 1940 the **17,000‑acre Indiantown Gap Military Reservation** was completed and leased to the U.S. Army, officially dedicated **March 3, 1941**.  
- **Last Years (pre‑WWII)** – About 300 buildings were disassembled and reassembled; a Victorian‑style range house (built 1890) was moved to Indiantown Gap in 1938.  
- **Soldier’s Field Project (2020s)** – The Pennsylvania Chautauqua Foundation restored the former training ground into a community green space, adding a walking path, a foot bridge over Conewago Creek, and interpretive markers. Volunteers continue projects such as native‑plant planting and meadow restoration.

> *Source:* FTIG article details the 1885 start, 1898 war mobilization, growth to 2,800 acres, transfer to Fort Indiantown Gap, 1940 completion, and the 2025 Soldier’s Field revitalization【www.ftig.ng.mil/About-Us/News/Article/4232222/mount-gretna-fort-indiantown-gaps-predecessor/】.

---

### 7. Summer Recreation Site Status

Mount Gretna is a **year‑round summer retreat** whose population roughly doubles in June–August. Key features:

- **Lake Conewago** – Victorian‑era bathhouse with high‑dive floating docks, sandy beach, swimming, canoeing.  
- **Porches & Front Street** – Iconic front porches define the town; strict rules limit lawn mowers and tree trimming.  
- **Recreation Facilities** – Roller rink (open‑air playhouse), miniature golf course, boating, kayak/paddleboard rentals.  
- **Entertainment** – Juried art shows (third weekend of August), jazz/chamber‑music concerts, lecture series, book reviews, “International Make Music on Your Porch Day.”  
- **Events Calendar** – Cooking lessons, nature walks, yoga, professorial talks, flamenco dance lessons, Rachel Carson reenactments, etc.  
- **Community Hub** – Post office serves double duty; many cottages lack mail delivery.

> *Source:* CBS News describes the “summer camp” atmosphere, the porch culture, and the double‑use of the post office【www.cbsnews.com/pittsburgh/news/pennsylvania-chautauqua-mount-gretna/】.

---

### 8. Attractions Over the Years

| Era | Notable Attraction |
|-----|--------------------|
| **Early 1880s** | Charcoal production for the **Cornwall Furnace** (iron for cannons for George Washington’s army). |
| **1883–1885** | Picnic grounds along the railroad; stone fountain. |
| **1885** | First National Guard encampment; “Switch‑Back” roller coaster, carousel, dancing pavilion. |
| **1889** | Construction of narrow‑gauge railroad by Robert Coleman. |
| **1892** | Hall of Philosophy (1909 built), Greek temple, Tabernacle, 100+ cottages, first Bible Conference. |
| **1909** | **Conewago Hotel** – 125 rooms, private baths, elevators, telephones, uniformed staff, “servants in uniform… and chefs from New York.” Terraced tennis courts. |
| **1910s–1920s** | Amusement park with carousel, switch‑back coaster, dancing pavilion; restaurants like **Kaufman’s Store & Hotel**, **Chautauqua Inn**, **Timbers Restaurant**. |
| **1930s** | Move of Victorian range house to Indiantown Gap; National Guard headquarters. |
| **1940** | Completion of Indiantown Gap Reservation; dedicated as a U.S. Army training base. |
| **1950s–1960s** | Decline due to automobiles; narrow‑gauge abandoned. |
| **1970s** | Revival via **Outdoor Art Show** (first 1976), chamber‑music/jazz series, “Culture Gulch” cottage community. |
| **2000s–Present** | **Soldier’s Field** restoration, **Timbers Restaurant & Dinner Theatre**, **Jigger Shop** ice‑cream parlor (operating since 1890s), **Gretna Theatre** (one of America’s oldest professional summer stock theatres). |

> *Sources:* Wikipedia geography section; official site’s “Our History” detailing early amusements and hotels; AP News describing the 54‑page program and 1909 Hall of Philosophy; Timbers Restaurant listing; Jigger Shop website noting operation since 1895; Gretna Theatre description as one of the oldest summer stock theatres【webpage_scraping】【jiggershop.com】【gretnatheatre.org】.

---
